Inside Maker's Mark brand identity by Turner Duckworth

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (355 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.
  • It has been revealed that the bottle does the talking.
  • The type comes from a person, not a library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turner Duckworth rebuilt the Maker's Mark brand identity around its red wax, casting Star Hill Farm materials into marks that tell the story.

It has been revealed that the bottle does the talking. Turner Duckworth kept the hand-dipped red top exactly where it belongs, at the center of the system, then built a whole language out of it. Wheat stalks, oak rings and native flora from Star Hill Farm were dipped and cast in the same red wax, so the marks that carry the brand are literal pieces of the place. Against a Wheat Cream ground, the red reads as one loud note in a quiet room, with Printmaker's Black holding the type steady.

The type comes from a person, not a library. Co-founder Margie Samuels shaped the original bottle, and the studio recreated her handwriting as a custom typeface with Nick Cooke at G-Type. Hundreds of characters, contextual alternates and ligatures keep it feeling handwritten rather than set, and her voice runs through the labels, menus and posters in a flowing, wax-like hand.

According to recent reports, layouts stay plain on purpose. A letterhead puts the Samuels family's SIV mark at the center and the distillery address in the corner, so place sits at the heart of every sheet. Type stays large and calm, with room around it, and the wordmark does its work without decoration.

According to recent reports, the palette is the bottle, remembered in three tones. Wheat Cream is the ground, true to the label. Printmaker's Black carries the type. Wax Red does the rest, in finish and in form: powder-coated metal, glazing and varnish applied to objects with smooth, flowing shapes. The same red runs across mugs, folders, books and table tents, so every object in the world feels dipped from the same pot.

Sources indicate that scott Grummett photographed the world at Star Hill Farm in warm cream tones and natural light, with touches of glossy wax red. The pictures tell the slower story behind the liquid: hand-rotated barrels, hand-cut labels, hand-dipped bottles, and the land that gives it flavour.

See more from Turner Duckworth.

  • It has been revealed that canon Rumors claims this is a known concern with Canon RF-mount extenders, where a lens can feel like it is locked onto the extender even when it isn’t.
  • It has been revealed that canon Malaysia’s notice on the matter is particularly interesting, offering slightly more information than the service notice from Canon U.S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, regional Canon offices worldwide have issued an urgent service notice regarding the company’s RF1.4x and RF2x extenders, commonly known as teleconverters. Canon warns that if customers suspect anything unusual about how their extender feels in use, they should request an inspection and repair through Canon.

It has been revealed that canon Rumors claims this is a known concern with Canon RF-mount extenders, where a lens can feel like it is locked onto the extender even when it isn’t. In some cases, a lens could even detach from the extender and fall to the ground. Given that extenders are commonly used with expensive telephoto lenses, this could be an extremely costly problem.

It has been revealed that canon Malaysia’s notice on the matter is particularly interesting, offering slightly more information than the service notice from Canon U.S.A. and others.

“We regret to inform that a potential matter has been confirmed for Extender RF1.4x/RF2x,” Canon Malaysia says, which goes further than what Canon U.S.A. writes.

According to recent reports, canon U.S.A. stops short of mentioning any issue, only issuing a “service notice” and noting that Canon RF extender users should always check the following:.

Canon U.S.A. adds that if photographers notice “anything unusual,” which could include the lens release lever feeling “stiff” or like it is “catching on something and cannot be operated smoothly,” there is a chance the RF lens is not locked in place.

“If used in this state, the RF lens may come off,” Canon continues.

Any affected users, or those who have any concerns about the operation of their RF extenders, should contact the Canon Customer Support Center in their region for an inspection and, if necessary, a free repair.

According to recent reports, in any case, it is not immediately clear what the exact issue is, what causes it, or how it might be fixed. Given that Canon is offering free repairs, though, it is reasonable to speculate that there is a physical component that needs to be fixed to ensure the consistently safe operation of Canon RF extenders.

Sources indicate that any photographers with Canon RF extenders should carefully inspect them before use and, if worried at all, contact their local Canon customer support team. A lens falling off an extender is a significant risk.

PetaPixel has reached out to Canon for comment and will update this story if it hears back.

#10203. Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown.
  • “We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” indicates Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the upcoming attribution.
  • The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, Fresh York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.

“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” indicates Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the upcoming attribution.

The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

Llanes Serrano says the road to the upcoming attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.

Industry observers note that the early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano notes that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.

Sources indicate that julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s new chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day notes.

Industry observers note that llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s new conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.

Greta Llanes Serrano treating the frame of the Frick's Della Robbia in the Frick Collection's newly built Sherman Fairchild Center for Art Conservation Photo: George Koelle.

In a recent development, the process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the latest 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she states. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.

A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.

Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

Industry News: Customizable and Colorful (Not Boring) Camera Nominated for iPhone App of the Year

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple declared its 2026 App Store Award finalists today, and a standout iPhone camera app earned a coveted nomination.
  • Recent findings suggest that (Not Boring) Camera is one of three finalists for iPhone App of the Year, and it’s easy to see why.
  • Industry observers note that “You’re gonna love how it feels,” claims the app’s developer, Not Boring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple declared its 2026 App Store Award finalists today, and a standout iPhone camera app earned a coveted nomination.

Recent findings suggest that (Not Boring) Camera is one of three finalists for iPhone App of the Year, and it’s easy to see why. The app, sometimes stylized as !Camera, features a fully 3D camera interface, extensive customization, and haptic feedback designed to replicate the feel of holding an actual camera.

Industry observers note that “You’re gonna love how it feels,” claims the app’s developer, Not Boring. “I guarantee it.”.

In a recent development, (Not Boring) Camera aims to be more than just a pretty face, though. Like other popular iPhone camera apps released in recent years, !Camera eschews AI processing in favor of a more natural imaging engine. Its proprietary SuperRaw mode promises “film-like tones” while preserving a photo’s “beautiful natural grain.”.

The app supports Apple’s ProRAW and Basic processing, plus it can save photos as RAW DNG files for editing in other apps, like Darkroom, Lightroom, and Photoshop. It also supports HDR image capture across four settings: off, low, medium, and high.

“!Camera is the first camera app to enable professional-level color grading with 3D LUTs (‘lookup tables’) used in high-end workflows by pro photographers to achieve realistic film simulations and unique cinematic looks,” Not Boring continues. The app includes photographer-designed LUTs, LUT importing, and preset creation tools. The organization regularly releases new styles and collaborations.

It has been revealed that the most recent collaboration is with the Tokyo-based art collective Nuevo.Tokyo. The AgBr style brings a vintage-inspired black-and-white look to !Camera.

The app also packs extensive manual controls—including exposure, shutter speed, white balance, ISO, and focus—alongside tools like focus peaking, zebra stripes, and a histogram. For finer focus adjustments, the virtual lens features its own “Precision Focus Ring” with a focus scale.

It has been revealed that customization extends to the look of the camera app itself. Customers can design a custom virtual camera by choosing colors for its body, top panel, lens, and buttons.

Sources indicate that if (Not Boring) Camera ultimately wins the award when winners are announced next month, it certainly won’t be the first camera app to earn the honor. In 2024, Kino and Adobe Lightroom were both honored among Apple’s Apps of the Year. Halide Mark II won in 2022, too.

Recent findings suggest that (Not Boring) Camera is available now for free. Access to all features requires a Plus membership, which is $14.99 per year or $59.99 for a lifetime license.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1061 w)

Latest Update: Lumix Has the Video Chops to Beat Sony, So Why Won’t It Even Try?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being unveiled.
  • For context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the firm opened with the L10 back in May.
  • And so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being unveiled. When he described the S1 II but in a box camera format, I couldn’t help but express my dismay. “That’s it?”.

For context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the firm opened with the L10 back in May. That felt like a proper start to what we assumed would be a full year of serious product debuts. This wasn’t an expectation we came in with; it was one that Lumix put into our heads: the company specifically said it had more planned for 2026 and that we should be excited.

And so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall. That is a major reason why I’m so disappointed by the SHX1. It’s not that the camera is bad or that it doesn’t have a core, dedicated audience. It’s more that this isn’t the camera that I was expecting to be the cap of a celebratory year where Lumix was poised to really strut its stuff.

The Lumix S1H has been languishing for years, and not because there isn’t a market for it. It just seems like Panasonic doesn’t know what to do with it. When the S1 II was revealed last year, that really felt like the case because the camera felt like it did everything we ever wanted the S1H successor to do.

But I argue that, even with all that known, Lumix — the brand known for video performance — has, for some reason, been unwilling to take on Sony in the highly competitive commercial camera space that is dominated by the FX series. For all of its strengths in video, Lumix appears scared: either of Sony or of the success that would come from actually trying.

In 2021, Sony confirmed the FX3 and, in one fell swoop, changed the game. It created the perfect camera for the mid- to high-end filmmaker at a really compelling sub-$4,000 price. It wasn’t part of the Alpha series, so Sony could fully focus on video performance. The FX3 is the logical conclusion to the success that the a7S series created, and it was (and still is) immensely popular.

As Jordan Drake put it in this week’s episode of The PetaPixel Podcast, the FX3 became the industry standard through its design.

“It became just the industry standard for if you’re doing event work or commercial work. Because it is such a recognizable camera – like that gray, with that pronounced, sharp-edged grip – when producers and directors and people see it, they immediately know that’s acceptable. That’s the massive thing I think Panasonic’s butting up against. An S1 II is every bit as capable but it looks like an old DSLR. And I think everybody wants to move away from that,” he indicates.

“The FX3 is just the visual language of a semi-professional small camera now.”.

Canon and Nikon got that memo, which is why the ZR and the R6V have that same visual design language. Panasonic Lumix has chosen to ignore that aspect of its cameras to its extreme detriment.

According to recent reports, compared to Sony, Panasonic’s camera division (it is now one division that combined Lumix and VariCam) is small, and maybe that’s to blame for these problems. Maybe it doesn’t have a good design department. That would make sense, since Lumix has not been a particularly good example of enticing camera design, and it’s very much hurting it now. I think it believes it should be able to stand out through performance alone, and that’s a lovely sentiment, but it’s just not reality.

Creators buy cameras that they want to be seen with, not just cameras that can do the job. You can argue that isn’t how it should be, but it is very much a reality.

It has been revealed that there is nothing wrong with the SHX1. It’s an excellent camera that will resonate with current Lumix filmmakers. Maybe that’s what Lumix wants: to keep its current audience happy.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s not what Lumix needs right now. To grow and find itself in more hands, Lumix needs to actually beat Sony at its own game – a game it is entirely equipped to win handily. I am a Lumix user and have been since the GH4. It’s reluctance to even try and take on the FX tier is incredibly disheartening, because I 100% would love to have an FX5-styled camera with Lumix guts.

Recent findings suggest that lumix’s in-body stabilization is better. Lumix’s record modes are, on the whole, better. I mean, the manufacturer was giving filmmakers open gate and in-camera anamorphic desqueeze years before it was even a twinkle in the other brands’ eyes. This is the space where Lumix should be king, but its refusal to go at Sony head-on makes it seem like the company is scared it might not succeed.

Or, worse, Lumix is scared of the success that would bring it. Maybe it doesn’t want that level of attention. Maybe it likes feeling like a scrappy underdog, and the idea of being a market leader is just too much pressure.

It has been revealed that whatever the case, as good as the SHX1 is, it’s not the camera Lumix needed to release in this moment. Sony was stumbling and tripping over itself with the FX5 launch, giving Lumix the perfect window to jump ahead if it were prepared for the moment. It clearly was not.

I get not being able to directly respond to the FX5, but the FX3? Five years later, how do you not respond to that? You, the video camera company? It feels like cowardice despite the timing not possibly being any better… which makes missing that moment even worse.

I don’t think Lumix fully grasps how badly they fumbled this opportunity. They might not realize the extent of this mistake for months or years. With the moment up for grabs, Lumix just chose not to reach out for it.

#10192. Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1892 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party.
  • Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions.
  • In a recent development, hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most notable artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.

Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a newly introduced dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.

In a recent development, hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most vital museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a upcoming institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.

Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

According to recent reports, raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareTiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.

Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870).

Credit: Museum of Fine Arts Budapest – Hungarian National Gallery.

Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)Hungarian National GallerySzent György térIn Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.

In a recent development, working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s fresh Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05).

According to recent reports, museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareThe MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.

Industry observers note that left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.

Hungarian crown jewels on display in the parliament building.

Photo: Schopenhauer; Courtesy Wikimedia.

Recent findings suggest that the Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)Hungarian ParliamentKossuth Lajos térThe Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.

A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.

Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969).

Hungarian National GallerySzent György térNow regarded as one of the most important artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.

Recent findings suggest that judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ SquareGoya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.

An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”.

Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial.

Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)Id. Antall József rkpIn the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.

It has been revealed that comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.

Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939).

© Museum of Fine Arts – Vasarely Museum, Budapest.

In a recent development, victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)Vasarely Museum BudapestSzentlélek térFor the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.

Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

© Szépművészeti Múzeum/ Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566).

Museum of Fine Arts, BudapestHeroes’ Square.

Hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.

Sources indicate that A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996).

Photo © József Rosta / Ludwig Museum - MoCA, Budapest.

© SUMUS Gáyor & Maurer Foundation.

Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)Ludwig MuseumKomor Marcell utcaDuring the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.

A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

Fujifilm Will Host an X Summit in Paris on December 2

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fujifilm has unveiled that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST.
  • “2026 is remarked to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm says.
  • Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in Fresh York City in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fujifilm has unveiled that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST. X Summits have traditionally been Fujifilm’s stage for announcing a new product, and given Fujifilm has not released an X-series camera this year, it could very much use one.

“2026 is remarked to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm says. “To celebrate two centuries of photographic history, and to honor all the photographers and photography lovers who have created countless inspiring images along the way, the next X Summit comes to you from Paris, France.”.

Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in Fresh York City in October. The last X Summit was held in Shanghai in June 2025, which saw the announcement of the X-E5 and 23mm f/2.8 R. Before that, the X Summit in Prague launched the GFX100RF.

Going 18 months between X Summits is extremely unusual, but getting one in 2026 at all feels like a gift, given how quiet Fujifilm has been this year.

There is no official word on what to expect out of this X Summit (of course), although the perception has been that Fujifilm’s flagship cameras are in dire need of a refresh: the X-Pro, X-T, and X-H cameras are long in the tooth now.

Industry observers note that A new camera launch would also be an opportunity to address the largest complaint Fujifilm has come up against: autofocus. To its credit, Fujifilm knows it’s a place it must improve.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re trying,” Yuji Igarashi, General Manager of Professional Imaging Group, Imaging Solutions Division, Fujifilm Corporation, explained to PetaPixel at CP+ 2026 in Yokohama. “We still believe it’s necessary to just continue to improve by algorithm improvement. And it’s not that we’re not doing it. We are continuing to work on it.”.

Speaking of future devices, Igarashi noted improved sensors and processors likely would help.

Industry observers note that “In theory, future devices will be much more advanced, with the consideration of higher processing speed. That would help us as well, but that wouldn’t help existing users, so we’re trying to do both — algorithm improvement plus device improvement.”.

Fujifilm will broadcast the X Summit live on its YouTube channel on December 2 at 4 AM EST.

#10189. Is Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Worth It? The Hidden Costs

Is Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Worth It? The Hidden Costs

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, what's your FI number?
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • It has been revealed that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Avg Spending Increase with BNPL.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term plans, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

It has been revealed that the "interest-free" label on short-term plans deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies reveals that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

Industry observers note that the financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

Industry observers note that A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL people have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound swiftly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

Industry observers note that the credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing intends to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

According to recent reports, there is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a fresh dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

In a recent development, the financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something crucial.

The question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how swiftly you reach FI.

Mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL looks — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing intends report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

Klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing aims charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently reveals that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most customers, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

In a recent development, buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL people spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Obsbot has unveiled the Tail 2 ADV, a latest 4K PTZR camera featuring a 21x optical zoom and custom LUT support.

The camera, which has already earned a 2027 CES Innovation Award, features a custom Type 1/2 image sensor with Dual Native ISO and support for 4Kp60 and 1080p120 recording.

Obsbot says the camera’s AI-powered image signal processing pipeline handles noise reduction and enables 4K HDR video at up to 30p with all-pixel phase-detect autofocus.

“All-pixel PDAF and Focus Over Zooming help the camera swiftly refocus on distant, stationary subjects as focal length changes during a zoom,” Obsbot claims.

Speaking of zooming, the Tail 2 ADV’s lens has an equivalent focal length range of 34-702mm and a variable aperture system. At the wide end, the aperture ranges from f/1.7 to f/7, while for telephoto shooting, it ranges from f/3.8 to f/7.

In Pro mode, camera operators can remotely adjust aperture, ISO, and shutter speed, offering greater creative control in changing lighting conditions such as stage performances, outdoor productions, and houses of worship.

The camera includes built-in subject recognition for autofocus tracking, identifying people, more than 30 animal species, and over 200 object categories. Using its pan, tilt, and zoom capabilities, it can automatically adjust framing to keep moving subjects in view. Operators can choose from six tracking speed settings alongside custom modes, as well as define preferred framing and tracking boundaries.

“These settings allow live production teams to determine not just which subject the camera follows, but how it executes the shot,” Obsbot explains. The camera can also roll thanks to its built-in gimbal, enabling native 4Kp60 vertical recording without cropping.

According to recent reports, for professional workflows, the Tail 2 ADV offers Obsbot Log—a proprietary logarithmic image profile that promises greater flexibility during color grading—alongside custom LUT support. Users can import and preview custom LUTs in Obsbot’s accompanying software, and the camera supports timecode and Precision Time Protocol (PTP) to sync with other cameras.

In a recent development, for connectivity, the Obsbot Tail 2 ADV includes 3G-SDI output up to 1080p60 and a full-size HDMI 2.0 output supporting up to 4K resolution. It also features Gigabit Ethernet, a 2.5mm RS-232 port, two USB-C ports, separate 3.5mm mic and line inputs, and a microSD card slot. The camera’s built-in 5,000mAh battery delivers over four and a half hours of operation, while USB PD 3.0 and PoE+ support allow for extended continuous power.

Industry observers note that the Obsbot Tail 2 ADV PTZR camera will arrive on December 8. Preorders are open now with a limited-time $200 discount, bringing the price down from its $1,599 MSRP to $1,399.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Instagram has introduced a fresh feature that allows people to edit Stories after publishing them without losing existing views, likes, or replies.
  • Announced by Instagram head Adam Mosseri, the update gives users a 15-minute window to change text, music, stickers, and drawings after sharing a Story.
  • Industry observers note that previously, consumers had to delete and repost a Story to correct a typo, change its caption, or add music they had forgotten to include.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram has introduced a fresh feature that allows people to edit Stories after publishing them without losing existing views, likes, or replies.

Announced by Instagram head Adam Mosseri, the update gives users a 15-minute window to change text, music, stickers, and drawings after sharing a Story.

Industry observers note that previously, consumers had to delete and repost a Story to correct a typo, change its caption, or add music they had forgotten to include. The latest feature removes that requirement, allowing edits to be made while preserving the post’s existing engagement.

The Verge notes that the ability to edit Stories was first spotted in development by reverse engineer Alessandro Paluzzi in April. It is now rolling out to customers. To make changes, users can open a published Story, select the three-dot menu in the bottom-right corner, and tap “Edit Story.” Edited posts will display an “edited” label when viewed by others.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Industry observers note that the change also addresses some of the complications associated with deleting and reposting Stories, particularly when they form part of a sequence. Re-uploading content can disrupt the original order of posts, while creators and social media managers may also be concerned about the impact of reposting on engagement metrics.

“A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” Mosseri indicates.

Alongside the editing feature, Instagram is introducing several changes to its Stories tools. These include new fonts, colors, and shapes for stickers, which will be organized into sticker sheets to make them easier to browse. The platform is also updating its multiple-photo selection process and adding new background options, including blur effects, colors and gradients.

Yesterday, PetaPixel reported on Instagram’s new tool that’s designed to help creators on the platform protect their work.

Called content protection, it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected.

#10182. Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1465 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • It has been revealed that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for significant works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • In a recent development, for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers mentioned that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

It has been revealed that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for significant works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

In a recent development, for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a newly introduced buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

Recent findings suggest that in the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

According to recent reports, subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” mentioned the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox said this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

In a recent development, also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that showed at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (Newly introduced York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

It has been revealed that several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read said that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

In a recent development, by and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which indicated small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

Sources indicate that while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Industry observers note that another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff stated she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

The gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff said.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery showed a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he mentioned.

The gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

According to recent reports, as many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," states the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

In a recent development, further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan said, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

In a recent development, meanwhile, concerns of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

Industry observers note that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

Legendary Photographer Ellen Von Unwerth Says ‘There’s No Money Left in Fashion Photography’

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, says there is no money left in the industry today.
  • For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.
  • However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, says there is no money left in the industry today.

For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.

However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.

“These days, there’s no money left in fashion photography,” Von Unwerth tells Fashion Network France. “It’s nothing like it used to be, when there were 10 pages in magazines and newspapers, and posters everywhere. You don’t see that anymore. You don’t see the big billboards anymore.”.

Recent findings suggest that von Unwerth explains that fashion photography has become less financially rewarding as brands increasingly direct their budgets toward events and influencers rather than traditional print ad campaigns. She notes photographers now face longer waits for payment, tighter deadlines, and less creative freedom than they had earlier in her career.

“Now, the money goes into events, influencers… So there’s almost no money left,” she adds. “You have to wait a very long time to get paid. And then they want the photos tomorrow — or even yesterday! Before, we were on our own on set. It was really just us, the photographers. We were the bosses; we did our own thing. It was our kingdom; it was secret.”.

It has been revealed that von Unwerth states fashion photographers have increasingly lost control over their shoots, with multiple behind-the-scenes [BTS] photographers and teams now working on the same set. She says this makes it difficult to establish who actually took a particular image once it is published. She compares modern fashion shoots to film productions, where a director oversees several camera operators rather than capturing everything themselves.

“Nowadays, there’s the BTS photographer. Then there are the BTS of the BTS. There are three other photographers doing different styles,” she tells Fashion Network France. “And I fought against that for a long time, but I’ve given up. Now there are five people taking pictures behind me. And you don’t know, when it comes out: “Is it my photo or is it someone else’s?” In the end, I just say it’s my photo! It’s like in the film industry: there’s a director, who oversees everything, and there are other cameramen filming.”.

Recalling a shoot for beauty brand L’Oréal, Von Unwerth says she became frustrated and ordered everyone to leave after discovering that around 50 people behind her were taking exactly the same photograph.

Von Unwerth’s comments come weeks after a report revealed that fashion photo studios are closing down as brands increasingly embrace AI thanks to the big savings offered by the technology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A trial over the long-disputed estate of Andy Warhol’s photographer Billy Name, including the rights to his extensive photo archive, finally begins this week.
  • Name became Warhol’s close collaborator and photographer in the 1960s.
  • His Factory-era photographs are regarded as some of the most important visual records of Warhol and the Pop Art movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trial over the long-disputed estate of Andy Warhol’s photographer Billy Name, including the rights to his extensive photo archive, finally begins this week.

Name became Warhol’s close collaborator and photographer in the 1960s. He lived in Warhol’s Latest York studio, the Factory, for seven years and became the artist’s in-house photographer. Using a Pentax Camera, Name captured thousands of iconic photos of Warhol, his art, and the stars who visited the Factory.

His Factory-era photographs are regarded as some of the most important visual records of Warhol and the Pop Art movement.

Industry observers note that however, when Name — who was born William George Linich — died in 2016, a legal dispute broke out over his estate, which included the rights to his valuable collection of photographs. More than a decade after Name’s death, the rights and fate of thousands of his photographs still remain legally contested.

According to recent reports, according to a report by Times Union, a newly introduced jury trial at Ulster County Surrogate’s Court in Ulster County, New York, will finally decide who has the right to license the black-and-white photographs Name took of Warhol and who will control the future of his extensive photo archive. The case will be the first jury trial over an estate that Ulster County Surrogate’s Court has ever presided over.

Industry observers note that the dispute is between Name’s longtime friend and agent Dagon James and his niece Suzette Linich both of whom claim to be the photographer’s rightful heir. At the center of the legal battle are two different wills left by Name. Linich presented a will dated 2011 that named her as the executor and sole beneficiary of his estate. Although the court accepted the document, James subsequently presented a more recent will, signed in 2015, that left the entire estate to him.

In a recent development, A key question in the trial is whether Name had the mental capacity to make the 2015 will. By 2014, the photographer, who is in his early 70s, was reportedly suffering from arthritis, diabetes, and depression and was frequently hospitalized. Name’s family argues that he was often confused and vulnerable to influence, alleging that James persuaded the photographer to exclude his relatives from his will.

It has been revealed that james disputes those claims, maintaining that Name was mentally competent, trusted him, and made a deliberate decision to leave him in charge of his photographic legacy. The attorney who prepared the 2015 will testified that Name had clearly expressed his intention to exclude his relatives from his estate and leave everything to James.

  • The gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentagram drew a full custom alphabet for Storefront Gala 2026, turning the Oyster Bar sign into loud, blocky, crayon-bright type.

The gala took over the Grand Central Oyster Bar on September 28, honoring artist Mel Chin, arts leader Deana Haggag, and the architecture firm SO-IL. Anyone who has eaten under those Guastavino vaults knows the sign on the wall. Rudolph de Harak packed its letters tight, rimmed them in heavy black outlines, and filled them with colors straight out of a crayon box. Against wood paneling and old tile, it has always looked like the one guest in the room who came to have fun. Pentagram started from a simple question: what would the rest of that alphabet look like?

The answer is a custom display typeface with a full set of letters and numerals. Strokes run broad, corners clip short, and counters turn angular. The O is an octagon with a diamond punched through its middle, and that shape sets the rules for every other character. Blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple take turns filling the forms.

Storefront Gala 2026 appears in compact stacks and stepped arrangements, with rotated numerals adding an unexpected twist. Letters meet along their black outlines and lock into continuous compositions that feel assembled from colorful building blocks. A smaller sans serif organizes the event information around these expressive forms, holding the honorees, the venue, and the date in quiet lines above the noise.

Industry observers note that the system runs across digital announcements, posters, a folded program, screen graphics, and embroidered caps. Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

It has been revealed that the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, yarrow is one of the most commercially successful photographers working today.
  • The Scottish photographer began his career in sports, covering the 1986 World Cup in Mexico for The Times of London, where he got a well-known shot of Diego Maradona holding the trophy aloft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fine art photographer David Yarrow has sat down with Graham Bensinger for a long chat about his career and life.

In a recent development, yarrow is one of the most commercially successful photographers working today. He’s probably best known for his dramatic, large-format black-and-white wildlife photographs, although he has moved into fashion, celebrity portraits, and staged scenes.

The Scottish photographer began his career in sports, covering the 1986 World Cup in Mexico for The Times of London, where he got a well-known shot of Diego Maradona holding the trophy aloft.

But as Yarrow tells Bensinger, he became disillusioned with sports photography after attending the Calgary Winter Olympics in 1988, fretting that it was too difficult to stand out from the many other photographers also covering events.

So in his early 20s, Yarrow pivoted and moved into finance. On 9/11, he made some bold market moves minutes after the first plane hit the tower, netting him significant bucks.

But Yarrow states his finance career eventually fell apart when Bernie Madoff’s massive Ponzi scheme was uncovered, and investors pulled all their money out of his business.

If there’s one photo that put a rocket in Yarrow’s career, it’s the great white shark breaching while hunting a seal that he took off the coast of Cape Town, South Africa.

A post shared by David Yarrow Photography© (@davidyarrow).

Yarrow claims he was with a picture agency at the time that sold it to newspapers and magazines around the world for him. It netted him roughly $16,000. The problem was Yarrow had spent $20,000 in the pursuit of that photo and so ultimately lost $4,000.

According to recent reports, but redemption was on the way in the form of a Texas lawyer called “Jaws” who wanted to buy the great white photo. When Yarrow quoted $6,000, the lawyer couldn’t believe how cheap it was.

“That was my a-ha moment, or my road to Damascus moment, or when the penny dropped,” says Yarrow. “That was when [I realized] one person could pay me more for a photograph than all of the newspapers and magazines in the world.”.

Industry observers note that petaPixel covered Yarrow’s team portrait of the Norwegian soccer team on their way to the World Cup in the U.S. last summer. Yarrow got the team, which includes star striker Erling Haaland, to dress up in Viking gear.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The growing use of AI-generated food images in Japan, a country with strict laws against misleading product photography, is raising concerns.
  • In much of the world, food photography on product packaging often exaggerates what is inside.
  • In Japan, food packaging must show the product exactly as it is even a tiny exaggeration is seen as misleading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The growing use of AI-generated food images in Japan, a country with strict laws against misleading product photography, is raising concerns.

In much of the world, food photography on product packaging often exaggerates what is inside. But in Japan, it is illegal for companies to use misleading food photos on product packaging.

In Japan, food packaging must show the product exactly as it is even a tiny exaggeration is seen as misleading.

According to recent reports, no fake ads. No chemicals. No adulteration. Just pure honesty in every bite. https://t.co/kFKP0n9a1c.

Sources indicate that — Dr. Rajeshwari Iyer (@RajeshwariRW) October 28, 2025.

Japan enforces some of the world’s toughest packaging regulations. Companies must ensure that the photos on their packaging accurately reflect the actual product, and failing to do so can lead to legal consequences. Any discrepancy between a product’s image and the real item is considered misleading. Even minor exaggeration or embellishment can be treated as a violation.

It has been revealed that under Japanese law, photos on product packaging are treated as factual claims. If a photograph on a packet of crackers demonstrates toppings arranged in a certain way, the crackers inside must match that presentation. The size, shape, and appearance of the product should closely mirror what is depicted in the image.

However, despite Japan’s strict standards for product photography, AI-generated food images are rapidly spreading throughout the country’s food and restaurant industry, prompting a backlash from consumers, according to recent reports.

In a recent development, an increasing number of food and beverage businesses are turning to generative AI to produce food images, menus, and promotional posters. The practice has frustrated some Japanese consumers, who say they deliberately avoid visiting restaurants that use AI-generated promotional images.

In one particularly example, a Japanese food truck went viral in the country after using AI images of a “tomato and scrambled egg rice bowl” that had a melted cheese pull look, despite the dish not having any cheese in it. Following online backlash, the food truck owner issued an apology and pledged to replace the AI images with real photographs.

It has been revealed that under current Japanese law, there is no requirement to disclose whether an image is AI-generated. However, in a country where the accuracy of product photography has long been subject to strict legal standards, the growing use of fake food imagery is raising questions about authenticity, consumer trust, and how far AI should be allowed to replace traditional photography and design.
