📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1144 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
  • According to recent reports, in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?
  • “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami revealed intends for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

According to recent reports, in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

Industry observers note that the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Industry observers note that those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

According to recent reports, “Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

Sources indicate that according to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch claims the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch indicates. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

In a recent development, the “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Sources indicate that beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto states, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

In a recent development, for the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”.

Canva Now Lets Users Turn Off Generative AI Features

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (358 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canva has introduced fresh settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.
  • It has been revealed that the generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes.
  • However, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canva has introduced fresh settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.

It has been revealed that the generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes. It also prevents consumers from generating images through Canva’s AI chatbot.

However, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform. Tools such as Background Remover and Magic Grab will remain available, even when generative AI is switched off. Canva says these tools will stay enabled because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything upcoming.”.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction is based on how the tools operate. While generative AI features create new content, Background Remover and Magic Grab work with existing images. The latter allows users to select an object within an image and reposition it elsewhere in the design.

A second setting allows users to reduce the amount of AI-generated material displayed in Canva’s content library. When enabled, the platform will prioritise human-created templates, graphics, and other design elements in search results.

Recent findings suggest that however, the setting does not guarantee that AI-generated content will be excluded entirely. Canva claims that a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated material, and designs containing these elements will carry an AI label in their metadata.

Both settings can be accessed through the profile menu. To disable generative AI tools, owners should go to Profile, select Settings, open Permissions, and switch off Enable generative AI features. To reduce AI-generated content in search results, they can navigate to Profile, Your Account, and AI Personalization, then enable the option to show less AI content.

It’s no secret that AI has a popularity problem, and Canva appears to be listening to that sentiment. Last month, PetaPixel reported that the company released an image generation model that wasn’t trained on photographs.

#10169. How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1814 w)

How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition.
  • The phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery.
  • A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition. The Munich-based company seems like an unusual collaborator for Honor, the smallest of the five major Chinese phone brands.

The phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery. A more substantive addition is the phone’s Arri Cinema mode, inspired by Arri’s Alexa cinema cameras, which we’ve already seen in the Honor Robot Phone. This presents an entirely different way to capture video on Honor’s flagship.

A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.

Arri’s history in analog cinema laid the foundation for its color expertise, though early on, the manufacturer essentially carried someone else’s color science since the film stock itself determined the look. Arri’s film scanner and film recorder, the Arri Scan and Arri Laser, became fixtures in studios, where engineers learned “what makes film look like film.”.

In a recent development, moving to digital cameras enabled Arri to study many different film stocks to build a single default look, supported by a logarithmic brightness curve and a custom color gamut. Thus came the “digital negative,” a flat, data-rich image meant for grading rather than direct viewing.

With skin tones as a central design goal, the firm states it photographed many faces to build a gamut that could consistently render varied complexions. That also means more stable color science when footage is over- or underexposed, with shadows that don’t veer into purple territory. This reflects years of feedback from colorists on how quickly they could achieve a finished look with Arri footage.

Sources indicate that for Honor’s part, this marks a first in that it was one of the only Chinese phone brands (along with Huawei) that, until now, hadn’t partnered with a European imaging brand. While not terrible, its previous flagships couldn’t produce the kind of video quality competitors were delivering. Partnering with Arri isn’t just about catching up, but about ultimately surpassing every competitor, including the iPhone.

Honor handles the pipeline, which is why its own H1 chip is an integral hardware piece. That chip works in the RAW domain for what it calls “lossless noise reduction and extra dynamic range.” Achieving “cinema-grade” dynamic range requires capabilities beyond what a standard mobile processor offers, which is why this dedicated silicon works in tandem with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. Honor reps were coy about how this particular marriage actually works under the hood.

According to recent reports, what we do know is that Honor’s team in France worked closely with Arri in Munich, which helped tune the image signal processor (ISP) by sending weekly software revisions during development. Beyond that, Arri personnel made no contributions to the phone’s hardware design.

According to recent reports, here’s what Arri has to work with in the Honor Magic9 Pro Max: The dual 200-megapixel main (24mm equivalent) and telephoto (85mm equivalent) cameras both have CIPA 8-rated stabilization. Arri Cinema mode records up to 4K at 60fps, supports a 2.39:1 or 16:9 aspect ratio, and has a base Exposure Index of 160.

Exposure Index (EI) is similar to ISO, though it functions differently on cinema cameras. Arri cameras normally work at the base setting for optimal dynamic range, which isn’t how it works on a smartphone camera given the smaller image sensors. The base EI is the setting where the camera’s designers determined the sensor captures a fixed range of light most effectively, delivering the best possible dynamic range. In practical terms, that means the phone needs more light to hit its sweet spot than an Alexa would, which makes sense for a much smaller sensor. Honor and Arri have to pull this off by warding off noise when shooting at higher EI settings in dim scenes.

Industry observers note that arri Cinema mode can shoot in LogC3, the logarithmic encoding used in Arri cameras before the Alexa 35, including colors that approach the LogC3 gamut. Honor claims both the main and telephoto cameras track the LogC3 curve almost perfectly, marking a first for Arri, which had never matched multiple sensors in a single device before. But there’s also a catch to exactly how this works.

Showing charts that compared the phone’s response against a real Arri camera, Arri notes the phone clips in the highlights because its sensor isn’t custom-designed like Arri’s own “expensive” ones. The sensors are also vastly different in size, making the phone’s dynamic range far more software-driven than it would be on an Arri camera.

Sources indicate that note that I only mentioned the main and telephoto cameras—because the Arri mode won’t work on the ultra-wide camera. Honor says it reluctantly left the lens out, citing vague time constraints since the partnership was only about six months old (at the time I visited). Rather than rush to get that out, it prefers to “get it right first” before committing to adding that lens. It’s just not clear whether that could happen through a software update or in a future device, since the main and telephoto cameras each required custom curves and color matching.

My own take is that tuning a third camera may cost more money than time, and given that this is Arri’s first attempt without its own sensors, it leaves the ultra-wide as the odd lens out. Even so, a wider focal range isn’t unfamiliar territory for Arri, given that its Signature Prime line includes an 18mm lens, so we’ll have to wait and see.

Inside the Arri studio—on a newly built set with both an Alexa and a Magic9 Pro Max capturing the exact same scene—the side-by-side clips look surprisingly close.

Recent findings suggest that looking at the footage from both cameras later on my own computer monitor and on different phones or tablets, Arri’s clips offer better clarity and gradations in skin tones, but not by the margin I’d expect given how vastly different the two cameras are. It’s fair to say these results not only compete with the likes of Vivo and Oppo, but also fire a real warning shot at Apple. I’m no longer convinced the iPhone is the smartphone video king.

Both Arri and Honor point to how they shifted the phone’s color patches (open circles for where the phone started, solid for where it ended up) so its output lands near a real Arri camera. The default look matches Arri’s pre-Alexa 35 cameras, with 14 built-in LUTs that are always available in Arri Cinema mode out of the box.

Recent findings suggest that adding LUTs is easy, with a comically high 87 looks available directly from either Arri or Honor online, all assembled from the tech giant’s Arri Media post-production house. These range from black-and-white variants that emphasize different color channels to period film emulations, seasonal grades, beauty, and teal-and-orange looks—all of which also work in DaVinci Resolve. Some are over-the-top throwbacks that might only fit very specific use cases.

While the sheer level of choice is undeniably substantial, it can quickly become a mess once you bring them in. Assuming you add all 87, you have no way of rearranging, organizing, or deleting any. Before long, finding the one you’re looking for becomes an almost endless scroll. You can also freely import custom LUTs from other sources—including any LUT built with Arri’s color science—which only adds to the clutter. I pointed this out to Honor reps, who noted they will see about fixing it.

Industry observers note that despite the potential for overcrowding the mode, Arri Cinema is a huge upgrade over what Honor had before. I’ve come away impressed not just by the image quality, but also by the versatility of the included LUTs, which make recording almost anything look interesting. Adding a film-like aesthetic that doesn’t feel like a papered-on filter is a factor, but so is shooting in Log with manual controls for creative license. Excellent stabilization and built-in audio controls help the cause. Tapping the microphone icon offers five directional options: Standard, Long-range, Close-up, Voice isolation, and Voice boost. They’re actually better than I expected, though you can still use an external mic if you want.

Industry observers note that the mode offers 4K or 1080p at 24, 25, 30, 50, and 60fps. It also supports the APV 10-bit codec, which, despite some compatibility issues, remains a viable ProRes alternative (thanks to smaller file sizes) when running those files through DaVinci Resolve.

Notably missing is 120fps, which is restricted to the standard Video mode and carries a dubious connection to Arri given the vague assurances I received. It’s not at all clear whether Arri’s color science is sprinkled in here, though my eyes tell me it’s not. What’s especially head-scratching is that the standard Video mode locks 4K resolution to the Vibrant style. Switch to any other style, and resolution drops to 1080p for reasons I can’t ascertain. A software update should easily fix that, but we’ll have to wait and see.

It has been revealed that it’s important to remember a key distinction in defining Arri’s role, which is based on image science, not optics. Despite making lenses and accessories for its own cameras, Arri isn’t involved in what Honor is doing on the optical end at this stage. So, unlike Xiaomi and Leica, Vivo and Zeiss, or Oppo and Hasselblad—which routinely collaborate on lens hardware—that isn’t the case for the Magic9 Pro Max.

Sources indicate that at its core, a cinema company teaming up with a phone maker is a commercial play. Arri reps note that cinema remains the company’s priority, even as the market for high-end cinematography shrinks amid falling competitor prices. Licensing Arri’s color science is a way to reach people who may never buy a cinema camera while making them familiar with Arri Looks and post-production workflows.

Sources indicate that arri tried this before by collaborating with Panasonic on software upgrades, including for the Lumix S1R II, GH7, and GH6, where Arri certified Panasonic’s implementation of the LogC3 curve. A smartphone partnership, however, is far more mainstream and exposes the brand to a much wider audience.

Industry observers note that I asked if we might see these color science changes apply to Honor’s still photography as well, but both brands were noncommittal. Arri reps admit they have little experience in stills but would like to see it happen, whereas Honor declined to discuss any roadmaps on that front. It’s not clear if the two brands signed a long-term agreement, but from the looks of it, they blueprint to collaborate on more than just a few devices.

The Filmmakers Behind ‘Primetime’ Printed the Entire Movie on 16mm and Rescanned It

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.

One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.

Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.

The crew used London-based Cinelab, which has a third-generation 16mm Cine-Mitchell recorder built in-house. Once the film print was created, it was scanned back into digital using an Arriscan, which delivers “perfect edge-to-edge focus.” The resulting footage was then regraded.

Sources indicate that “Primetime is also a period film, in a way, and working with the film print helped make the visuals far more immersive,” notes Bolen. “Any feeling of artifice in the image seemed to disappear after printing to film.”.

However, the film wasn’t shot entirely with the digital-to-film-to-digital method: Oppenheim and Bolen utilized a few obscure, frankly bizarre, cameras as they searched for a way to recreate that early 2000s aesthetic and also communicate the plot to the audience.

Recent findings suggest that one such camera was a 2005 MiniDV camera, the Panasonic AG DVX 100B. Bolen used this for the hidden camera shots, and it is a very similar technology that was used to film the original show, To Catch a Predator.

In a recent development, “These cameras are a challenge, because unlike modern cinema cameras, they can’t shoot in a LOG color space,” Bolen claims. “We didn’t really alter their baseline settings; we decided to lean into the cameras’ built-in contrast. To Catch a Predator has such a strong look, and we tried to match it as closely as possible in-camera. Even in the final grade, we made very few adjustments.”.

But that distinct look posed a problem in the editing room: how to blend the shots taken by different cameras together. After all, DV cameras are not cinematic.

Industry observers note that “We couldn’t get them to match,” says Bolen on the Mark Bone YouTube channel. “Like, no matter what we did with the settings, some would skew red, some would skew green, on some the exposure seemed off.”.

But Oppenheim didn’t care and threw the rules out of the window. In fact, he would film the same scenes on different cameras, and then in the edit, choose whichever one he liked.

Speaking of other cameras, there were two more that Oppenheim and Bolen used: a Plumbicon tube camera and a medical camera — the kind used for colonoscopies.

Archer Green points out that the Plumbicon tube camera actually dates back to the 1980s.

It has been revealed that “It was meant to serve as a ‘spiritual’ camera rather than a period-accurate one,” Bolen writes for American Cinematographer. “These cameras use vacuum RGB tubes that split light into red, green, and blue, and the beautiful thing is that the tubes age and burn out over time. In a way, it’s a camera that feels like it has a soul — it decays over time, just like a human does.”.

The creators of ‘PRIMETIME’ explain how they shot a scene using a 480p colonoscopy camera 🎥🤯https://t.co/Z8m4aT7YM0.

— Complex Pop Culture (@ComplexPop) September 27, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that for one of the close-ups of Pattinson, Bolen used a doctor’s colonoscopy camera. The crew even built a rig to hammer home the effect.

“That was a scary one because that camera does shoot 480p and I was like, ‘How am I going to get this approved?’ But to A24’s credit [the film distributor], they were like, ‘this is awesome’,” Bolen notes.

In a recent development, “There are no rules. We don’t have to shoot 6K. 480p looks awesome on the significant screen; I love it. It’s my favorite part of the movie.”.

According to recent reports, "Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

Recent findings suggest that the good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

Industry observers note that the IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:.

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits.

In a recent development, the resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Sources indicate that important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Industry observers note that let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 1: Calculate Combined Income.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

It has been revealed that sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

In a recent development, beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:.

It has been revealed that the remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

Recent findings suggest that the FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

According to recent reports, this is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

In a recent development, example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

Recent findings suggest that the math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Recent findings suggest that every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:.

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Sources indicate that delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

Sources indicate that if you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Sources indicate that compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

Recent findings suggest that for the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

Sources indicate that for single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

Industry observers note that no. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

It has been revealed that no — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Sources indicate that yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

According to recent reports, social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

It has been revealed that there have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Sources indicate that yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Fresh York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • Sources indicate that but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Latest York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s Fresh York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

Sources indicate that but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in Fresh York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across Latest York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s revealed that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

Industry observers note that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

Industry observers note that estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Industry observers note that soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s Upcoming York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a newly introduced auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

Halide’s iPhone Duo Update Embraces the Crease and Adds an XL Mode

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, halide has declared version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo.
  • Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded.
  • “On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, halide has declared version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo. This includes a fresh “XL” mode that is designed for two-handed operation, as well as a feature that doesn’t avoid the crease, but instead embraces it.

Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Halide notes this feature, called XL mode, allows for “powerful two-handed operation.”.

“On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill. In low-light, the latter gives you a softer alternative to the built-in flash,” Halide adds.

“While apps like Apple’s own camera app expand the viewfinder to take up the full screen, it’s impossible to do this without obstructing your shot with camera controls. That poses a challenge when composing shots, so we’ve taken the approach of keeping the viewfinder clean.”.

Beyond just making these changes that take advantage of the two form factors the Duo offers, Halide went one step further and specifically engineered an interface for when the Duo is half-folded. The tech giant says that while most are avoiding the crease that appears when the phone is folded, it went the opposite way and embraced it.

Recent findings suggest that “Back when the iPhone X introduced in 2017, we were the first app to ’embraced the notch’ by putting histograms in the ears of the phone. Today, we think we’re the first app to ’embrace the crease,’ placing the histograms in the fold, an otherwise no-man’s-land of interactions,” Halide states.

By default, Halide’s camera controls sit on the same side as the camera itself. Tapping the arrows in the sidebar, the left and right sides swap, turning Halide into a waist level viewfinder.

Halide provided a few sample images taken with the updated Duo app:.

Halide usually doesn’t take long to update its app when new hardware lands, and even though the interface for this Duo-specific update feels like it should have taken a lot longer, it really isn’t too far off from what Halide provided for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro launch. When it dropped version 3.2, which gave support for variable aperture control, that arrived on October 2, which is about three weeks after the iPhone 18 Pro landed on store shelves. This update for the Duo comes just shy of a month after the Duo rolled out on October 23.

Halide version 3.4 is available starting today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ACDSee Photo Studio has declared version 27, which brings a bunch of newly introduced features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.
  • According to recent reports, version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the company says can find and group photos together by how they look.
  • “AI is shaping the future of photography and it’s our goal to lead the way in that space,” Frank Lin, CTO of ACD Systems, indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ACDSee Photo Studio has declared version 27, which brings a bunch of newly introduced features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.

According to recent reports, version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the company says can find and group photos together by how they look. These new options don’t compromise non-destructive editing, either.

In short, ACDSee has embraced AI editing.

“AI is shaping the future of photography and it’s our goal to lead the way in that space,” Frank Lin, CTO of ACD Systems, indicates. “With ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27, we’re bringing generative AI directly into the creative process, making it easier to find, organize and transform images while giving photographers the flexibility and control they need to bring their vision to life.”.

The bulk of the updates to version 27 are AI-focused, with the top-billed new feature having the highest chance of being the most controversial: image generation.

“Turn a text prompt into an image, choose a preset visual effect, or bring in reference images to guide character, style, and composition, right inside the photo workflow,” ACDSee notes. AI generation isn’t latest for photography tools, as Photoshop has had it for years now, but it’s not necessarily something that photographers are specifically asking for in a Lightroom competitor. Still, it’s here now.

Industry observers note that ACDSee appears to be following Adobe’s lead with the next feature, as it now supports editing via prompting. Photographers can describe a change in plain language or “use reference images to guide the look, and reshape a photo without a single brush stroke.”.

The AI search tool looks to be an alternative to Excire Photo and will find photos visually related to any primary target, with no keywords or tagging required. Images can also be grouped by similarity.

ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27 is available for $119.99, including 10,000 AI Credits for generative AI tools and 100GB of cloud storage.

This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (402 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • Sources indicate that meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. People can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

According to recent reports, the app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

Industry observers note that hyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a latest concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

It has been revealed that lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

Recent findings suggest that however, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

Iraq’s national museum introduces reopening after major renovations

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December.
  • According to recent reports, several vital artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry.
  • The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the fresh government under Ali al-Zaidi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

According to recent reports, several vital artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the fresh government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are looks afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

It has been revealed that A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has declared that a new museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

It has been revealed that al-Dakhili has also announced that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement states.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • In a recent development, mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

In a recent development, mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

He was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

Sources indicate that “Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

Sources indicate that “I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack noted. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

According to recent reports, “My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

It’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the company than he was.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it said too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it said too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The new mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit shows something new.

The wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Recent findings suggest that underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

This is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that highlights the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

Sources indicate that the floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

Industry News: Edward Noted Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis.
  • It has been revealed that while Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice.
  • Sources indicate that maiken Baird’s fresh documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die.

It has been revealed that while Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice. In one scene, Abdul Shafi, sitting at a nondescript table, is asked by an interviewer: “Is it your belief that if a Palestinian state was created, there would be lasting peace in the Middle East?” Just as he’s about to respond, the film mischievously cuts away, in an edit loaded with meaning. Palestinians may be seen in Western media, the film is telling us, but they cannot be heard from.

Sources indicate that maiken Baird’s fresh documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves. Like Salloum and Suleiman, Baird also sifts through reservoirs of found footage, though the result couldn’t be more different. Offering a rough chronology of Said’s life, Baird’s film celebrates him by highlighting his contributions and lasting influence in numerous domains, from literary theory to American foreign policy.

It has been revealed that for decades, the Columbia University professor of comparative literature was the most famous, if not the only, Palestinian regularly speaking on American airwaves and writing about the Palestinians in its magazines. Wearing his bespoke suits and contributing classical music criticism to the Nation, Stated cut an urbane, sophisticated, and cosmopolitan figure.

But it was his substance, and not his style, that earned him his legacy. As the author of the foundational text Orientalism, Noted was one of the most influential intellectuals of the 20th century, and he took the vocation extremely seriously, holding the yes-men intellectuals of the powerful in contempt. As he wrote in his essay “Secular Criticism": “It is not practicing criticism to validate the status quo.” For Said, an intellectual must always oppose domination while cultivating resistance to oppression.

It has been revealed that I am one of the fortunate ones. I knew Edward Said personally, having studied under him while I completed my PhD at Columbia University. With Andrew Rubin, another of his students, I edited The Selected Works of Edward Said: 1996-2006 (2019). (A producer of this film contacted me during its early phase for a background discussion on Said and his life, but I had nothing to do with the making of this documentary.) It’s hard to believe that more than 20 years have passed since Said died from leukemia in 2003, but thanks to Baird’s documentary, a fresh generation can now access his indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight for justice.

In a recent development, with the question of Palestine currently assuming a new urgency around the world, and with Israel’s genocide of Gazans ongoing, the timing of the film feels like a deliberate intervention. To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation. It’s no mistake that, aside from hearing a few interviewers’ questions and small asides, the audio of this 108-minute film consists almost entirely of Said speaking.

Produced with the cooperation of the Said family, the film includes moments from early home movies taken by Wadie Said, Edward Said’s father. The elder Said purchased a movie camera in 1938 and made “incredibly boring” films, according to the younger. By including snippets of these early scenes, Baird does something more than show us a young and gangly Edward Said. The home movies not only invite viewers into the private life of a Palestinian family in Palestine. They also become an assertion of presence against an ideology which demands Palestinian absence.

Young Edward was entirely apolitical. As a teenager, he was expelled for being a “troublemaker” from Victoria College in Egypt and sent by his family to the “puritanical” Mount Hermon School in rural Massachusetts, where, as he says, he was mocked endlessly for his name (“Ed Mentioned. Well, what did he say?”). An elite education at Princeton and Harvard followed, and then a job as an assistant professor at Columbia University. “The professional thing took care of itself,” he says. But after the humiliating Arab defeats of the 1967 war, Said felt a need to reconcile the two parts of himself: an American professor of literature and a Palestinian Arab born in Jerusalem. In the wake of the losses in 1967, his friend Ibrahim Abu-Lughod invited him to contribute an essay to the United States-based magazine The Arab World, and Said wrote “The Arab Portrayed,” his first significant foray into the politics of representation.

In the film, Noted describes his decisions to take on the Palestinian cause, and his father’s caution to his son: “I’m very worried about what the Zionists will do to you." In the early 1970s, while living in Beirut, he immerses himself in the Arabic language and literature and associates with some of the preeminent Palestinian intellectuals of the era. The film’s tempo picks up as Said’s star begins to shine more brightly. We watch him being asked borderline racist questions in multiple TV interviews, see him with Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat, and despair with him when the Israeli invasion of Lebanon leads to the expulsion of the PLO from Lebanon in 1982.

Remarked was the most prominent dissenting Palestinian voice to the 1993 Oslo Accords. He believed the PLO had sold out the Palestinian national movement, only to become “Israel’s enforcer” of the occupation. Baird’s film successfully shows how he went from being a fierce critic of American and Israeli policy to a fierce critic of American, Israeli, and Palestinian leadership. I knew Said at this time in his life, and what the film doesn’t show is the profound sense of isolation he felt while the entire global liberal establishment was telling us that “the conflict,” as it’s euphemistically called, was about to be solved. Needless to say, Said was right.

According to recent reports, music was a grounding force in Remarked’s life (he was a near-concert-level pianist) and another constant in the film. Baird ends her film with his growing friendship with the Argentinian-Israeli composer Daniel Barenboim. Said and Barenboim began the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra, a musical venture bringing together young Arab and Israeli musicians, in 1999, the same year his essay “The One-State Solution” was published in the Fresh York Times. The essay argued that “real peace can come only with a binational Israeli-Palestinian state.”.

In the final years of his life, Said committed himself to such efforts at coexistence. The last scene of this finely tuned documentary is of him playing the piano with passionate intensity. “It’s not our destiny to be refugees," he says via voiceover. "It’s not our destiny to be prisoners of war. It’s not our destiny to be commandos. It’s not our destiny to be an army of occupation. We have a choice.”.

There is more than a whiff of optimism in these later positions, and it’s impossible to say where Mentioned would stand today, as Palestinians face their most demanding fight for survival yet. But the fact that his optimism feels somewhat dated today probably tells us less about Said and more about how far away we are now from attaining true and lasting justice for the Palestinians.

Edward Remarked: Between Worlds (2026), directed by Maiken Baird, is screening at various film festivals including the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, London Palestine Film Festival, Marrakech International Film Festival, and many more. It will be released widely in 2027 by Kino Lorber.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with more creators capturing both photos and videos, accessory makers are stepping up to meet the demand. Heipi’s fresh 2-in-1 hybrid tripod head for photo and video promises the best of both worlds.

Photographers often like ball heads because they are versatile, easy to adjust, and stable. By loosening the head, photographers can swiftly recompose their shots. However, ball heads are not as easy to control or as smooth for panning motion as a traditional pan-tilt fluid head, which videographers typically prefer. Further, Heipi says its latest head also delivers the balancing performance of a gimbal head, a popular choice for wildlife and birding photographers with huge, heavy lenses.

According to recent reports, “Today, the line between photography and videography is becoming increasingly blurred. During a single shoot, creators may switch between wide-angle and telephoto lenses, move from still photography to video, and capture a wider range of perspectives and moments,” Heipi writes on Kickstarter. “Yet different shooting needs often call for different support equipment: a ball head, a gimbal head, a fluid head, and more. Carrying multiple heads adds bulk to your gear and extra weight to every journey.”.

Heipi believes its fresh hybrid head offers all the benefits of separate tripod heads in a single package.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head weighs 560 grams (just over 1.2 pounds) and is about the size of a traditional ball head. However, it can instantly switch from ball head mode to pan-tilt mode, and videographers can screw on a grip for even more control.

Heipi’s upcoming tripod head also features a stepless counterbalance system designed for gear weighing from 1.5 to 5 kilograms (3.3 to 11 pounds). That encompasses a wide range of equipment, including those massive, heavy supertelephoto lenses mentioned earlier.

Recent findings suggest that the KB50 features a standard 3/8″-16 UNC female thread on its base, allowing it to attach to a wide variety of tripod legs. It also includes an Arca-Swiss clamp.

The Heipi KB50 2-in-1 Hybrid Head is available to back on Kickstarter now, starting at $428, which is a $120 discount compared to the $548 MSRP. Heipi claims it will begin shipping in April 2027. With just over 40 days left in the campaign, Heipi has already shattered its $10,000 goal.

💡 Key Takeaways
