  • Superb environmental storytelling and art direction.
  • Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Funny, sad, euphoric… GTA 6 is the most entertaining and emotionally engaging open world I’ve played. Rockstar has taken the sandbox freedom of Grand Theft Auto and the environmental storytelling of Red Dead Redemption 2 and made something that feels lived-in. The characters, humour, and systems are all wonderfully written, and the attention to detail makes Leonida a place I want to stay in long after I’d finished the story. The set pieces rival Hollywood, but I'll remember the small, unplanned moments.

An extraordinarily detailed, living open world.

Jason and Lucia are brilliant protagonists.

Hilarious, unpredictable emergent gameplay.

Superb environmental storytelling and art direction.

The 30fps frame rate won't suit everyone.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Format: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S.

In brief: 5/5. Grand Theft Auto VI (reviewed on PS5, out 19 November) is the most convincing open world I’ve played.

Industry observers note that I laughed out loud multiple times within minutes of starting Grand Theft Auto VI. Not a chuckle or a smirk, but proper laughs, grinning ear to ear, as a particularly large resident of Leonida giggled, ran, stumbled, staggered and tripped over a railing into the river below. It was ridiculous and completely unexpected, and I loved it.

Industry observers note that we've waited 13 years for GTA VI and from the opening credits, Rockstar has crafted a hyperreal but intensely personal world where every corner of Leonida and Vice City offers a surprise. I've been playing for three weeks, finished the story, seen some endings, and I'm still playing to find out what random secrets Leonida has left to share. Much of it has nothing to do with the fate of Lucia and Jason, GTA VI's modern-day Bonnie and Clyde. (Read our GTA VI coverage for more on the game.).

Driving around, you'll spot Just Stop Oil-style protests blocking traffic, teenagers dropping rocks onto motorway cars, or posters and flyers that lead to mysteries and new characters to call from your iFruit phone's contacts list. These aren't side quests in the traditional sense, with a marker on your map and a list to tick off; they're connections to random people, and the sense that this world exists beyond the screen.

Recent findings suggest that those teenagers dropping rocks? I detoured to teach them a lesson. Later, I stopped for someone posting for social media while balancing on a bridge, and failed to save him when he fell, and I actually felt bad. I pulled over for some teens daring each other to jump from a bridge into a river, decided to show them how it was done, and while I was swimming, they stole my car.

According to recent reports, it's not risk and reward; it's just life in Leonida. It's incredibly fun.

The scale of GTA VI is incredible, but not in the usual sense of a vast map to cross. It's the depth and detail that gets me: the branding, signage, store shelves of snacks and comic books that can be read, snatches of conversations from passersby muttering about their lives or something they heard on the radio, the same thing I heard on the radio. Most buildings can be broken into and explored, and I've spent far too long sneaking into warehouses that have no obvious reason to exist beyond making the world feel authentic and the possibility that something of value could be snaffled away inside.

In a recent development, shops, bars and clubs are lovingly detailed, and once inside you're free to toy with the world. Buy something, drink something for a stat bonus, steal something, change your clothes, or earwig and people watch. Sometimes you'll need to change outfits, because it throws off the cops chasing you; sometimes just because you feel you should wear beach clothes on the beach, because I'm completely hooked into this world.

According to recent reports, the geography is considered too. Vice City is a maze of overpasses and winding spaghetti motorway junctions; the city itself is a muddle of back alleys, malls, and beachfront hotels, while the roads out in the country are simpler and more relaxed; the swamps need care to navigate; the sandy, wooded isles of the north are a stolen boat. Beaches, swamps, forests and distinct neighbourhoods all have their own character, and you feel it: stressed in Vice City, calm and playful up north, the mullet of map design, if you will. Even the residents and police behave differently depending on where you are.

Industry observers note that early on, Jason and Lucia visit a rich, enclaved community filled with jewellery shops, polished pavements and high-fashion stores practically demanding to be robbed. A policeman on a bicycle stops them and warns them that their kind isn't welcome. I pushed my luck, choosing confrontational dialogue options, refused to obey, and he called in backup from other pedal-bike cops who made it clear our kind wasn't welcome. I returned at night and stole everything, and it felt so good.

Giving you an emotional reason to do things is one of GTA VI's biggest successes. You start to understand the people who live here, the divisions between communities and the little injustices that make you want to cause trouble.

In a recent development, there's always something happening, too. An armoured car is robbed, so I follow it to the thieves' hideout and steal everything. A farm sign notes 'pilot wanted', so I drop in and end up in a whole side story about meth-strawberries that eventually riffs on a Marvel character I never expected. Leonida's residents are 'Karens on crack', too. Scrape someone's car, and they'll chase you down; look at someone too long, and they'll demand a fight; drive down a motorway, and hyped up teen will lean out of their car to challenge you to a race. Once I planned a bank heist, only to find a random gang shooting the place up, and I got caught in the melee. It's layer upon layer of random, living events, and even on a mission, it's easy to get sidetracked as gunshots ring out.

GTA VI rewards your downtime too; it wants you to simply enjoy the place and the moment because conversations eavesdropped on in a bar are hilarious but also tease secrets about the world, whether residents are complaining about the weather or arguing over culture-war nonsense raised by the State's shock jock, who is furious about that weekend's Manatees football result and the demise of 'mansculinity'. Some can be engaged with and will share random but useful news about Leonida.

There's no Ubisoft-style checklist here. Stunts, hidden collectable cards (which you can sell in-game), fishing challenges and sporting events are there if you want them, but the world grows as you explore, meet people and build up your contacts list. You just exist in Leonida and enjoy exploring, competing and completing things.

The weather is a major part of that experience, because it looks beautiful – golden morning sunlight cuts through thick mist over a wildflower meadow with realism, dramatic storm clouds and dense golden fog engulf a city skyline, obscuring buildings and bridges in an atmospheric haze.

But weather also affects how you engage with the world. Days feel long enough to play in, different things happen at different times, and the weather is dramatic and distinct. That hazy mist can obscure your visibility, while hard rain can limit distance and disrupt sound, something used to dramatic effect in a nighttime kidnapping rescue where large halogen lights pierced the rain and mist, creating drama but affecting line of sight in some spaces.

Recent findings suggest that likewise, a plane handles differently in wind, rain and cloud, as the controls judder and inputs feel less responsive. Flying through a storm, with lightning sparking and rolling across the horizon, gives you a real sense of place and moment but also puts you slightly on edge.

Jason and Lucia's relationship really surprised me in GTA VI, and it's one area where Rockstar picks up where Red Dead Redemption 2 left off. Both are well-rounded protagonists with motivations and shared dreams that you help build. Lucia is alive and sprightly, Jason is dour and determined, and how their connection develops, or doesn't, becomes a game of its own.

A subtle romance and empathy system is at play. How much time the pair spend together, the conversations you choose, the dates, time at home (yes, you can make love in the shower, on the sofa, in the kitchen and, well, all sorts of places) and even how and when you proposal and commit crimes all feed into how their relationship develops, and it can affect how their story ends.

Recent findings suggest that what you do on a job matters too. Kill lots of people, and you get a different criminal rating than if you spare lives, and the duo seem to have a healthier relationship if you play to control a room with threats or shoot to injure rather than murder. I wanted a loving crime couple, so almost without meaning to, I started shooting people in the legs and arms to make them fall or drop their guns instead of headshotting everyone in a room. I wanted my Lucia to like my Jason.

According to recent reports, likewise, when Jason went undercover as 'the poolboy' for a saucy film shoot, I held back on how far I took things. Lucia was getting madder in my ear as Jason applied lotion to an actress, and when given the choice to go all in, as it were, I pulled out, as they say, as it were, because I wanted Lucia to still like Jason. I still don't know how far you can take that mission, but this is Rockstar, so I imagine it's all the way (and that's what she said).

Few games get that emotional connection right. It doesn't come only from good writing and characterisation, but from all the little conversations, actions, reactions and animated moments when they meet up or succeed. You'd have a heart of stone to go out of your way to ruin their romance, because you can. You monster.

Controlling when and how they meet up is part of GTA V's character-switching development. Moving between them is nearly instantaneous: the camera pulls out to a global view, zooms back down, and you can message the other to hook up or tell them to meet you somewhere. And you do get committed: when I occasionally Irish-goodbye'd Jason, I felt the need to call him and check up.

The central narrative picks up what worked in Red Dead Redemption 2, splitting the story into chapters that each introduce a upcoming gang or cast and a grand setup to blueprint towards. The structure gives you plenty to play with, and the story spans more years as the couple bounces from backwater crimes to epic, militarised heists. These feed into cinematic tentpole moments that draw on everything from the later Fast and Furious movies to Assault on Precinct 13, with even a little nod to Die Hard as Lucia sparks a lighter in an air vent, laughs and paraphrases the classic line, "Come out to the coast, we'll get together, have a few laughs.".

Sources indicate that it's also where Rockstar's love of a good heist movie really shines. Some of the bigger set pieces have the clockwork precision of an Edgar Wright film, with different characters, objectives and moving parts all working towards one carefully choreographed finale. The editing is part of the fun: the action cuts between Jason and Lucia as they tackle their separate jobs, each sequence dovetailing with the next as the initiative unfolds, the clock ticks down, and the stakes rise.

The grand finales of each chapter are proper spectacles that never play out the same way and deliver 'cinema'. You might be flying gunships over a stormy ocean, or swapping between Jason and Lucia as they complete different parts of a larger initiative. Jason races to a rooftop to stop mobster reinforcements while Lucia hacks a vault, and you're jumping between the two as the action cuts back and forth, the tempo building with each switch. One moment you're holding off a gang; the next, you're working through the other side of the operation, and it all clicks together like clockwork. It's a wonderfully cinematic way to make character switching part of the action, not just a convenient way to get around the map.

Around these set pieces that take time to build are lower-key missions, some tailored to each character, and this is where Rockstar earns its rewards. The satire of modern America, social media, celebrity culture and consumerism that we love about GTA is here in abundance. A favourite is a storyline in which Lucia becomes embroiled in a bored-housewives vape cult that's like Goop meets Elizabeth Holmes.

It has been revealed that then there are the random encounters that make Leonida feel active, and never run how you think. An elderly woman screaming for help on a back road took me to her farmhouse, where I expected a robbery or a rescue. Instead, a client had 'died' in a bondage orgy gone wrong, and I needed to dispose of the body in a river. Even that didn't end as I expected.

Recent findings suggest that even 40-plus hours into the main story, Rockstar finds fresh ways to surprise me. It introduces a vault-hacking mini-game that uses haptics and controller prompts for one bank job, then drops in a drug-dog sidekick for a single mission. Ideas are picked up, enjoyed and dropped before they go stale. GTA VI has so many that it never has to hang around with one for long.

Shooting and weapon handling are superb, and each gun feels distinct. The cover system and enemy AI respond nicely even in busy rooms, and stealth is reliable and effective. While the massive set-piece story missions can feel a little restrictive and scripted because they need to reach the cinematic heights Rockstar is aiming for, anything can happen outside them.

Industry observers note that A bank heist, for example, needs proper planning. Park a getaway car, choose the right vehicle, pick the rear door lock, hack the cameras, wear a disguise, and don't overstay your welcome. The world is so well designed and systematised that everything feels connected. Next time, go in through the front door, or steal a truck and pull an ATM from the wall. Heists in backwater towns are easier because there are fewer police around. And nothing plays out quite as you expect; every bank is unique, and after two seamless jobs I go for a third and it all goes wrong – an unexpected teller wanders into the office for a coffee, an alarm is tripped, and before I realise it, I'm shooting my way out, bags shouldered, and looking for a new car to steal… the best-laid plans are shot.

The police react to all this more deeply than in previous GTAs. There's no longer just a star rating and a zone to escape, but how you escape matters. Swap cars and clothes, and they'll lose you, because they're looking for your description, not you, me, the player. All the old tricks are still here, from roadblocks and air support to increasingly aggressive police AI, but you have new ways to shake them off beyond just driving fast.

It ties into car ownership too, another Red Dead Redemption 2 influence. You can't carry everything, so it's worth stowing a change of clothes and weapons in your car. Carrying a gun openly gets the police involved, but some Vice City passers-by will also decide to take you out as well.

Driving feels familiar from GTA V, but with enough nuance to feel like an evolution, as cars have different weights and handling, and each one reacts differently through the DualSense triggers: sports cars resist less than family saloons when you pull to accelerate. Boats, bikes, planes and helicopters all work as you'd expect, but even here there are subtle shifts in how responsive each can be – one helicopter I stole was uncontrollable and spun into the swamp.

Character models, facial animation, skin, hair, and clothing all deliver the hyperrealism I expected from a new GTA, though they're still larger-than-life caricatures built to feel relatable rather than photorealistic.

Animation, including the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes, is where GTA VI takes its biggest strides. Lucia and Jason are wonderfully handled, whether it's the little snuggles and embraces or the way they hold up a bank and play off one another, but the breadth of animation across GTA VI is what impresses. Every Leonida resident feels uniquely animated, and it's fun just to people-watch. Early on, a drunk girl follows Jason around a bar and is authentically annoying, and the nightlife feels realistically overwhelming. Bar bands are animated to sell their next song, and even the wildlife has moments: I watched a white-tailed doe and buck nuzzle each other lovingly and naturally through Jason's rifle scope. It was cute enough to make me take a breath, but Jason needs more money, so the shot rang out and the wildlife scattered.

In a recent development, leonida has a recognisable visual identity, bold and vibrant, with every corner full of quirks, from the deep forests of the north to the out-of-town mall and rows of copy-and-paste suburban houses. Fictional adverts, billboards, shops, signage, and TV build the world, as if you see an ad for a beer or car, and you can buy it (or steal it). Beyond signage, graffiti walls, sculptures, exhibits, and more invite you to linger and just take in the world.

It also feels like a realistic evolution of the 1980s Vice City I knew and loved, a city with a history inside a broader world, with references to Liberty City aplenty, from car number plates to Jason and Lucia's accents. It's somewhere to wallow, whether you're having a cocktail under palm trees swaying in a breeze or tearing up Vice City in a neon-lit supercar while crypto bros trade and wannabe rappers parade.

It's a wonder this all runs on a base PS5. I remember the mess of equally ambitious games like Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, but GTA VI is in a different league. The frame rate is locked at 30fps, and it's fine: stable, with little slowdown or stutter, and controls and handling feel spot on. There's occasional soft pop-in, but few visual compromises or trip-ups. You can feel the work that's gone into making everything run smoothly, and GTA 6 is polished to perfection.

Sources indicate that I'm really only scratching the surface. Familiar street races, bank heists, and chilled fishing and hunting trips are joined by crypto rug pulls, golf tournaments, and deep-sea treasure hunts. Or I just drive, hunt a swamp thing, stop to solve a mystery from a local ad, or relax with a game of pool and a Patriot beer. You can take on the State's sports and races, go sailing, or listen to 80s FM hits, the biggest dance tracks, or to the MAGA-inspired Richard Bastion Show – "more volume than logic" – who's mad about everything.

Sources indicate that this game has video games inside it that feel more complete than some real games I've played, from the top-down sci-fi shooter Time Jackers: Rewind to a lightgun score-chasing bar game Bang For Your Buck. And in typical Rockstar fashion, they all have a satirical edge, like the indie auteur game Tenebrae Lux, which pokes fun at the po-faced walking sims that were all the rage: it's black-and-white, minimal, and filled with overwritten prose like a Taylor Swift song about metaphors.

Industry observers note that GTA VI is a world that exists beyond its main story, where everything feeds into and off each other. It's the best world-building I've experienced in a game in years, partly because its systems all work in a coherent, purposeful and layered way, but also because it's not afraid to be weird, whether that's discovering the dumpster lawyer, becoming a frog, slobbing on the sofa and watching an episode of Whose Dick's Whose, or finding an influencer in the boot of a stolen car who wants to be kidnapped for clout.

Recent findings suggest that there are minor restrictions, mainly when the big cinematic missions take over and funnel you down a more scripted path, but for good reason, and the 30fps cap won't suit everyone (yet it's really not an issue). But in a game that otherwise gives you this much freedom, they're the exception.

Recent findings suggest that 13 years? The wait has been worthwhile. I still set off with a proposal, get distracted by something ridiculous at the side of the road, and lose another hour to a game I thought I'd finished. I laughed within minutes of starting, and I laugh every time I play. I've also been stressed, revolted, astonished, baffled, heartbroken and euphoric. I've run the full gamut of emotions, and I still do each time I return to Vice City.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

“Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials,” remarked the studio.

“In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment,” it added.

“Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself.”.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna’s structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site’s natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Industry observers note that timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

“Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework,” said the studio.

“Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest,” it added. “The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself.

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Options+ is context-aware and offers presets for popular apps.
  • A good alternative to native drawing tablet remotes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smart, compact control surface with real potential, the Logitech MX Keypad has plenty of presets and context-aware functions for the best software and utilities, but you’ll only get your money’s worth if you put in the setup time.

Options+ is context-aware and offers presets for popular apps.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Keys: 9 customisable LCD keys, 15 pages.

Connection: Wired USB-C, 1.5m USB-C to USB-C.

Dimensions: 91.7 x 77.9 x 25.5mm.

Features: Logi Options+, app-specific, automatically switching.

Compatibility: Windows and macOS.

Supported apps: Adobe Creative Cloud, Figma, Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, VS Code, IntelliJ, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Zoom, Slack, Google (beta), and more.

Recent findings suggest that I’m always drawn to gadgets that promise to save time or make things easier and more accessible, whether it's the best drawing tablets, shortcut keyboards, or odd little controllers parked next to my mouse: if it claims to shave seconds off a repetitive job, I want to try it. Photoshop is my worst offender, because half the battle is remembering where Adobe has hidden things this time with each newly introduced enhancement.

It has been revealed that the Logitech MX Keypad is a desktop control pad with nine customisable LCD keys, each showing an icon for whatever you’ve assigned to it. Two physical buttons flip between pages, so you get more shortcuts without another huge peripheral crowding your desk. It's in the Logitech MX line, gadgets aimed as much at creatives as at everyday folk looking to make life easier.

Sources indicate that at $99.99 / £89.99, it’s not an impulse buy but something you should consider, and after years of drilling Ctrl, Alt and Shift combos into my left hand, I wasn’t sure I needed one. I also use a drawing tablet and stylus for art, so I have just enough buttons on the pen, or I can access more on my tablet's virtual keyboard. But knowing a shortcut and having a button for the thing you hit countless times an hour, whether it's in Photoshop, calling up Google files or browser pages, is a different matter. That's where the MX keypad aims to be a decent all-rounder for everyday work and creative projects alike.

Nine square keys sit in a three-by-three grid, and because each has its own screen, the icons change based on what you’ve assigned. That beats a traditional macro pad with fixed labels: you can see what a button does instead of memorising obscure combos.

It works with the best digital art software and creative apps, including Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom, Premiere Pro, and Figma. Importantly, it’s context-aware, so you can select your app in Logitech Options+ and it loads presets for that software’s most common tools; from there, you can edit or set up your own actions.

Nine keys run out fast, so using up to 15 'pages' of nine preset buttons (135 total assigned actions) earns it keep as a feature. Overkill, yes, but some will want all that power at a button press. The Options+ app lets you build separate layouts for different jobs, one for Photoshop, another for Lightroom and so on. Rather than living with Adobe’s shortcuts, you build the layout around how you work, and it's as easy as going into the Options+ app and assigning keyboard shortcuts to the buttons, including combinations of buttons, and it supports different saved shortcut collections, so you can also tailor favourites to different apps.

At roughly 92 x 78 x 25mm, it sits beside a mouse and keyboard without taking over, and it's easy to hold, which matters if your desk already hosts a pen tablet or display. A kickstand and a 1.5m USB-C cable come in the box.

It’s not perfect. The keys lack the click of good mechanical keys, but they do have an old-fashioned soft-push feel, much like an old 90s dial-up digital phone, but that also means you need a little force to push one, and the stand lacks weight or 'stick', so it drifts as you press. The solution? Hold it by the top and depress with my thumb. I do like how each button has its own little digital decal icon showing its function, and you can buy sticky pads to keep it in place.

It’s also wired only, which is a little surprising at this price, but it's not the end of the world, and the cable is long enough for most setups.

For me, the MX Keypad makes the most sense with Photoshop (I've also downloaded and set it up for Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, Google, and Slack), and even fast keyboard users end up wishing something were easier to reach. Favourite brushes, colour swapping and fresh layers all suit the MX Keypad, and you can split them across pages for selections, masking, painting, and layer management. I’m a light Photoshop user, but I found that adding shortcuts for Lasso selections, favourite brushes, and layer options sped up how I use the software.

When I’m drawing, I don’t want to look down at the keyboard or lift my hand off the tablet, so a few key actions right beside my drawing area help. For the most part, I find the custom buttons on a stylus work well alongside touch controls on a tablet, but if you are more professionally minded and need all the options all the time, a shortcut keypad is essential. While XPPen, Huion, and Xencelabs all offer good remotes, the MX Keypad is a step above, with more buttons, more configuration options, and easy-to-understand icons and button labels.

Sources indicate that if you’re already quick on a keyboard, reaching across to press a button may not be any faster. The gain is in the visual reminders and having rarely used commands grouped on pages somewhere easy to find. With only nine keys, you’ll need to proposal your pages carefully, but for serious users, once organised, you'll be able to cycle to function collections at speed.

According to recent reports, of course, not all apps are supported; for example, Rebelle and ArtRage aren’t here, but you can add the apps manually and set up profiles and shortcuts based on keyboard commands; it just takes more time than Logitech’s preset app library. Using presets is as simple as clicking a drop-down menu, but adding and editing a fresh app setup and customising each key can take around 30 minutes per 'page'.

Because profiles are set per app, the buttons change colour and icon designs as you switch software. I found this to be the MX Keypad's strength, because it becomes one device that can follow you around your creative workflow, so if you’re someone who works between software, from Blender to Photoshop, for example, the MX Keypad can follow along.

Options+, the same app used by the MX Master 4 Special Edition mouse, can configure everything, but it takes some time to get used to if you’re editing a new app that isn’t supported out of the box. If you use the most popular, most common software, it’s easy; if you use niche apps, it can feel far from plug-and-play, since you have to manually enter each keyboard command.

For artists and designers who bounce between the biggest and most common apps, it’s a compact way to build your own control pad, and LCD keys beat cryptic labels on a standard macro pad or half-remembered keyboard shortcuts.

At $99.99 / £89.99, the Logitech MX Keypad is a fair price for a quick key remote. By comparison, the Xencelabs Quick Keys cost a similar $99.99 / £95.90 and also have LCD icons, but only words and no images, while the decent XPPen Remote is $49.99 / £49.99 but more basic than both Xencelabs and the Logitech. Both are wireless remotes, unlike the MX Keypad, but as a shortcut remote, the MX Keypad is the best of the three because Options+ offers an easy setup with established software and a huge number of buttons and pages.

Sources indicate that but the MX Keypad has more going for it than those remotes: more custom buttons, more context-aware presets, and the option to use ‘pages’, which packs a staggering number of functions onto one face. The significant advantage over a traditional drawing tablet remote is two-fold: you get little icons that explain each function, plus the depth of Options+ with multiple pre-loaded shortcuts for the best graphic design software and art apps out of the box.

Do beginners and hobbyists like me need this much choice? I mostly use two to three apps, for example, and three or four functions, and I don't need speed, but if you're a pro with a library of art, design, 3D, and video editing software to pair with and move across in one project, it would be a good gadget. For pros and tinkerers, it’s essential; for everyone else, it may be overkill.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.
  • Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.
  • The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

Industry observers note that “Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”.

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

In a recent development, “Bianni was born from the idea of giving latest life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” said Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”.

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

It has been revealed that “No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she mentioned. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

  • Hoptman joined the Drawing Center in 2018 following eight years as a curator in the department of painting and sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College (CCS Bard) has given its 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence to Laura Hoptman, executive director of New York’s Drawing Center. She will receive $25,000 and will be honored at CCS Bard’s spring gala in April.

Hoptman joined the Drawing Center in 2018 following eight years as a curator in the department of painting and sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). While at MoMA, she oversaw major traveling exhibitions devoted to Isa Genzken (2013) and Bruce Conner (2016), as well as the museum’s hotly debated survey of contemporary painting, “The Forever Now” (2014–2015). Related Articles Hamza Walker Wins CCS Bard's 2026 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence Frank Walter Escaped Racism and Violence by Looking to the Stars.

In a recent development, after beginning her career as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum, Hoptman worked as an assistant curator in MoMA’s department of drawings from 1996 to 2002. In 2003 she guest-curated “Drawing Now: Eight Propositions,” featuring more than 200 representational works by 26 contemporary artists, at MoMA QNS, and in 2004 she was director of the 54th Carnegie International in Pittsburgh. Between 2006 and 2010 she was senior curator at the Latest Museum in New York, where she co-organized “Unmonumental: The Object in the 21st Century” (2007–2008) and “The Generational: Younger than Jesus” (2009).

The Audrey Irmas Award has been given annually since 1998 and recognizes “groundbreaking visionaries in the curatorial field,” according to a press release. Past recipients include Adriano Pedrosa, Connie Butler, Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, Thelma Golden, and Okwui Enwezor.

It has been revealed that “Laura’s longstanding curatorial practice has furthered newly introduced art historical analysis and international recognition of drawing as a creative medium and social practice,” said CCS Bard executive director Tom Eccles in a statement. “Her international projects have reexamined the legacies of an array of artists through new and creative frameworks. What is often forgotten is how consistently Laura has demonstrated a boldness and bravery in championing artists across many institutional structures.”.

#10122. Latest Update: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

Latest Update: Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • Industry observers note that at present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll.
  • In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, by now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

Industry observers note that at present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting consumers’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He states this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

It has been revealed that “We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”.

Industry observers note that sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

Industry observers note that “During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In a recent development, in general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

Sources indicate that but GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, notes Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.).

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu claims losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

Sources indicate that as mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she indicates. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying problems may benefit sexual health.

Sources indicate that that means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

Sources indicate that “Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.).

In a recent development, GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, claims Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, notes board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

In a recent development, of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

Recent findings suggest that “Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he notes. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”.

According to recent reports, for those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon notes. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

Sources indicate that “Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer indicates. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”.

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec states, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Sources indicate that not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”.

In a recent development, if you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

In a recent development, working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The organization mentioned the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” remarked Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

It has been revealed that “It’s crucial to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”.

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler says can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

It has been revealed that A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while users can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

Users’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health said Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of newly introduced devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of his forthcoming Creative Time commission at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, artist Guadalupe Maravilla will offer a bevy of programming beginning December 18.

Titled Consejos de las Estrellas and presented in collaboration with the Clemente Soto Vélez Cultural and Educational Center, the project comprises a sculptural installation that will “serve as a healing instrument and a place to find warmth and belonging when the holidays deepen the feeling of absence,” as Maravilla told ARTnews when the project was announced in October. Related Articles Guadalupe Maravilla to Stage Major Installation at New York's Cathedral of St. John the Divine This December In Venice to Install Work for the Biennale, Artist Guadalupe Maravilla Alleges Racial Profiling by Police.

Recent findings suggest that core to Maravilla’s sculptures is their ability to be activated for sound baths, and Consejos de las Estrellas will offer eight sound baths during its run. Two of them will be staged in tandem with two winter holidays: a Christmas Eve Midnight Mass sound bath, beginning at 11:59 p.m. on December 24, and Latest Year Cleansing sound bath on January 9. The latter event will be proceeded by an herbal cleansing workshop by Herban Cura, which describes itself as a “healing justice herbalism and ecology school,” per its website.

A cancer survivor himself, Maravilla has long held sound baths specifically for the cancer community and he will offer two at St. John the Divine that will bookend this part of the programming. The first of these, on December 18, will be specifically for cancer survivors, healthcare workers, and caregivers and realized in partnership with the Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center. The final one will be staged on February 4, which is also World Cancer Day.

Consejos de las Estrellas will also feature performances by artist-collaborators who will activate Maravilla’s installation. They are Holland Andrews (January 22), Tesora Garcia and Camilo Godoy (January 29), and Jesús Hilario-Reyes (February 6). Maravilla will hold an artist conversation and Tarot reading on January 14.

Industry observers note that additionally, there will be a Three Kings Eve celebration and procession on the afternoon of January 5 with puppeteers from Teatro Sea. The project also will serve as a mutual aid hub, collecting food, clothing, and toy donations during its open hours, Wednesday to Sunday.

Consejos de las Estrellas will be open at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in Newly introduced York’s Morningside Heights neighborhood from December 17 to February 7. Opening hours will be Wednesdays to Fridays from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturdays and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m.; the project will be closed from December 31–January 2. Full details for the accompanying programming, which is free and open to the public, can be found on Creative Time’s website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live.
  • I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a fresh wellness trend making the rounds on social media.
  • There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a fresh wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

There’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

According to recent reports, it seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

Recent findings suggest that fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” says Fertz. “You are born young.”.

Recent findings suggest that it turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sources indicate that sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky says. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”.

Industry observers note that at school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Recent findings suggest that research indicates that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

In a recent development, “I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”.

According to recent reports, even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

Italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

Industry observers note that “Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”.

It has been revealed that paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very vital to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

Industry observers note that at cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in New York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert claims. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”.

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

The antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

It has been revealed that in Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

It has been revealed that “Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo claims. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”.

Sources indicate that indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Industry observers note that italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

“The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz notes. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, plan outings, and get out of the house.”.

It has been revealed that according to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz notes, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.
  • Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.
  • The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a latest public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a latest quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” mentioned Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”.

In a recent development, the retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with newly introduced glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” stated Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has named the Dutch-born curator and art critic Krist Gruijthuijsen as its next director. He will succeed Rein Wolfs in July 2027.

Gruijthuijsen, a self-described “artist-driven curator,” will join the Stedelijk from EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art in Finland, where he has been director since 2025, a role he holds concurrently with curator at large at Kunsthaus Zürich.

In a recent development, his vision for EMMA, a respected but relatively low-profile institution outside the Nordic region, included sustained support for artists through project funding, acquisitions and stipends, among more. Speaking to Frieze, he said he envisioned opening up the floor of the Brutalist building by removing its internal walls. Related Articles Dutch Art Historian and Curator Rudi Fuchs Dies at 84 'I Live for My Art. That's Really All There Is to It': Read One of Yayoi Kusama's Final Unpublished Interviews.

Prior to EMMA, Gruijthuijsen was director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, beginning in 2016. His tenure there included well-received programming, with exhibitions by artists such as Hanne Lippard, Beatriz González, and Hassan Sharif. He also curated “Martin Wong: Malicious Mischief,” which the Stedelijk co-produced and hosted from November 2023 to April 2024.

His return to Amsterdam will also mark a curatorial homecoming, as Gruijthuijsen cofounded the Kunstverein Amsterdam with Maxine Kopsa and served as its director from 2009 to 2012, a role that briefly overlapped with his time heading the MA Fine Arts department at Amsterdam’s Sandberg Instituut (2011-16).

At the Stedelijk, he will oversee the institution’s modern and contemporary art and design strategy and guide collection management and public engagement.

Sources indicate that “The [Stedelijk] has long held a special place in my personal and professional life, as it does in the history of modern and contemporary art and design,” Gruijthuijsen mentioned in a statement. “Its remarkable collection and rich legacy carry a responsibility that extends far beyond preserving the past. Above all, they call on us to engage with the present and help shape what lies ahead, with art and artists at the heart of everything we do.”.

He continued, “An essential part of my role will be to deepen the museum’s relationship with Amsterdam: to make it ever more open, engaged, and connected to the city and its communities. I want the Stedelijk not only to reflect the world we live in, but also to actively contribute to shaping its future.”.

In a recent development, airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:.

Industry observers note that the savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

Industry observers note that one important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

Industry observers note that the old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

Piaget’s Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch

💡 Key Takeaways
